final_candidates.decision_summary: K119 forms the essential Schiff base with the PLP cofactor; substitution with alanine definitively abolishes cofactor anchoring and catalytic transsulfuration.
Replacing the catalytic lysine with glutamate introduces a negative charge that repels PLP and disrupts the active-site electrostatic network, eliminating activity.
G307S is a canonical pathogenic homocystinuria mutation in an active-site loop whose steric disruption confers a severe loss-of-function phenotype.

stop_reason.detail: Top-3 mutations provide deterministic catalytic and structural disruption sufficient to abolish CBS enzyme activity.

history.rationale: Lys119 is the essential catalytic residue that forms the Schiff base with the pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (PLP) cofactor; alanine substitution directly abolishes PLP binding and catalytic competence.
K119 forms the essential Schiff base with PLP cofactor; replacing it with alanine completely abolishes catalytic transsulfuration.
Charge inversion at the active-site PLP-binding lysine disrupts cofactor positioning and electrostatic stabilization, abolishing enzymatic activity.
Introducing a negative charge at the PLP-binding lysine directly prevents cofactor binding and catalytic activity.
Gly307 is located in a tightly constrained loop adjacent to the active center; G307S is a classic pyridoxine-unresponsive homocystinuria mutation that causes complete loss of catalytic function.
G307S is a classic severe homocystinuria pathogenic mutation that severely disrupts the active site loop and abolishes catalytic activity.
Ile278 is a hydrophobic core residue in the catalytic domain; the I278T pathogenic substitution impairs folding and leads to severe loss of CBS activity.
I278T is the most prevalent homocystinuria mutation, severely impairing active-site conformation and tetramer stability.
Thr191 resides near the active site pocket; mutation to bulky methionine causes severe steric clash and abolishes catalytic activity.
T191M is a well-established severe loss-of-function homocystinuria mutation affecting core domain packing.
Cys52 serves as an essential axial heme ligand in human CBS; substituting it with alanine disrupts heme coordination and destabilizes the active holoenzyme.
C52 is a heme axial ligand; while mutating it impairs heme binding and allosteric response, basal PLP activity may partially persist.
His65 is the second axial heme ligand; alanine substitution disrupts the hexacoordinate heme architecture required for functional structural stability.
H65 coordinates heme as the second axial ligand; its loss alters regulation but is less definitive for total loss of catalytic function than active-site PLP mutations.
Arg336 participates in critical structural salt-bridge networks within the catalytic core; pathogenic R336C mutation severely compromises enzymatic activity.
R336C causes severe clinical homocystinuria with major loss of enzymatic function.
